summary: A 1970 proposed moratorium on changes to the network protocol, by R. D. Bressler. It suggests pausing changes so that implementers can build against a stable specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 72 proposes pausing most changes to the network protocol while sites finish implementing it and the system begins operating. It would still allow discussion of major design problems and extensions.

subtitle: A proposal to pause most protocol changes while implementation proceeds.

tldr.problem: Protocol changes can force sites to revise hardware and software already under development, delaying an operational network.
tldr.mechanism: The author proposes a six-month moratorium, or one lasting until the system is running and its characteristics can be observed, while allowing major problems and extensions to be discussed.
tldr.outcome: The proposal would defer changes limited to efficiency or implementation ease and keep new ideas available for possible later implementation.

facts.label: Proposed moratorium
facts.value: 6 months or until the system is running and observed

today: The unit metadata records RFC 72 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC is a proposal for a moratorium and does not state whether it was adopted.

sections.title: The Cost of Changing an Implemented Protocol
sections.content:
Robert Bressler says changes to the established protocol would affect hardware and software work that had been underway for more than 6 months at some sites. In the case of Multics, programs were complete or in advanced debugging.

The author argues that sites had agreed the protocol was workable and had begun implementation, even if it was not ideal.
sections.plainLanguage: Some sites had already spent months building against the agreed protocol. Changing it could force them to revise work that was complete or being debugged.

sections.title: What the Moratorium Would Allow
sections.content:
The proposal is a moratorium on most changes for the next 6 months, or until the system is running and its characteristics can be observed. Changes that only improve efficiency or ease of implementation should wait.

A major design problem should still be brought forward, as may an extension to the existing system. The author says details of the present system should not otherwise change during the moratorium.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed pause would defer efficiency improvements and implementation changes. It would still allow discussion of major design problems and new extensions.

sections.title: Why Wait for Operational Experience
sections.content:
The author argues that the network should become operational as soon as possible so people can develop uses for it. He says changes can be judged more clearly after actual operation, because a feature may prove unworkable or a proposed improvement may address the wrong problem.

New ideas should still be raised and discussed, but the author suggests labeling them as proposals for post-moratorium changes rather than immediate implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal is to get the system running and learn from its use before making nonessential changes. People can still discuss ideas and consider implementing them later.
